title: Developmental Delays: Trust Your Gut, Don't Wait and See
hook: If something about your child's development worries you, say so early. Routine screening and prompt action — not waiting and seeing — give kids the best shot, because early intervention helps.
key_points: You know your child best: bring concerns to the doctor early instead of waiting to see if they pass.
Acting early matters if your child isn't meeting milestones, loses a skill they had, or you have other worries.
AAP recommends formal developmental screening at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month visits, plus autism screening at 18 and 24 months.
Early intervention services support kids at home, in school, and in the community — and you can refer your child yourself.
content_html: When something about your child's development nags at you, the most important move is to speak up early. The CDC's guidance is direct: you know your child best, and if your child isn't meeting one or more milestones, has lost a skill they once had, or you simply have a concern, act early rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own.
extra_html: Two kinds of attention matter. Developmental monitoring is the informal tracking anyone can do over time, while developmental screening is a brief, validated questionnaire given by a professional — the AAP recommends general developmental screening at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month well visits, with autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. Per the CDC, identifying delays early helps children and families, because early intervention services support a child at home, in school, and in the community. You can ask the doctor for a screening, and in the U.S. you can refer your child directly to your state's early intervention program. This is general educational information — talk to your pediatrician about any worry; raising it early is never an overreaction.

related.title: Developmental Milestones: The Big Picture
related.hook: Development happens across several areas at once — social, language, thinking, and movement — and milestones describe what most kids do by an age, not deadlines every child must hit.

related.title: Well-Child Visits: Your Regular Check-Ups
related.hook: Well-child visits aren't just for when something's wrong — they track growth and development, deliver vaccines on schedule, and catch problems early, even when your child seems perfectly fine.

flashcards.prompt: At which visits does AAP recommend specific autism screening?
flashcards.explanation_html: AAP recommends general developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months, with autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'wait and see' the wrong approach to a developmental concern?
flashcards.back_html: Acting early gives kids the best outcomes — early intervention services support development at home, school, and in the community. If your child isn't meeting milestones, loses a skill, or you're worried, talk to the doctor right away.
